title: Work Back and Split
context: Grade 5, the worked examples on squares and Exercise 8.2's harder questions. An adult sees division and square roots. What the pages are doing is asking what number times a known measure gives the total, and checking by multiplying back, and building a larger area out of rectangles and equal squares whose areas add.

writeup.why: Work back to the side of a square from its area or its perimeter, find a missing breadth from an area and a length, and find the area of a figure built from rectangles or equal squares.
writeup.look: A target card over the working area, a square that grows with the Try dial, a perimeter string on the second phase, a rectangle with the Breadth dial on the third, and an L-shape with the Cut tool on the last.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Work Back and Split' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of tries made. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The target card stands at x 120, y 220, 300 by 90, deep blue, labelled Given. The figure lies below it at x 120, y 330 inside a box 600 by 360, drawn to one scale on squared paper. The Try dial and the Breadth dial are round dials at x 800, y 260; each try draws its rows in violet, labelled Row, against the target's near-black outline, and rows that fall short leave the outline showing while rows that spill past it are lit amber. The Fold in four button stands at x 800, y 360. The Check line runs along y 700 from x 120. On the fourth phase the Cut tool snaps a dashed line along a grid line, the two rectangles slide apart by 60 with their sides labelled, and the Join button at x 800, y 450 slides them back. The Copies control stands at x 800, y 540. The answer reached is green. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with cm, m, sq. cm and sq. m keys. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the ten tools of this chapter share them. The lengths the question gives, as a side, a length, a breadth, a height, an edge or a base area, are deep blue, labelled Given or by their own name. The perimeter, area, volume or missing side the working reaches is green, labelled Answer. The boundary that a perimeter walks round is vermilion, labelled Boundary. The unit being counted, one unit square, one unit cube, one row or one layer, is violet, labelled Unit square, Unit cube, Row or Layer. The part squares of an estimate and the space left over where no whole cube fits are rose, labelled More than half, Half or Left over. The side, square, cube, layer or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open, and nothing on this stage is ever grey. A square or cube that is not being counted stays warm white inside its near-black outline, grid lines, unit words and signs are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last figure stays drawn with its rows, the working line under it ending on the answer in green, and the check line beside it.

source_tool.description: A target card at the top of the working area gives the measure the question hands over, deep blue, labelled Given. For a square, a Try dial sets a side, and the stage draws a square of that side filled with violet rows, labelled Row, with the product side x side written under it; a try that falls short leaves the target's outline showing round it, and a try that overshoots spills past it. A perimeter string, vermilion and labelled Boundary, can be folded into four equal sides with a Fold in four button. For a rectangle, the length is drawn and labelled, and a Breadth dial stacks rows until their count meets the area, with a Check line that multiplies back. On the last phase an L-shape lies on squared paper; the Cut tool snaps a dashed line along any grid line, the two rectangles slide apart with their sides labelled, and a Join button slides them back as their areas add. A Copies control lays equal squares side by side. A number pad types a side or an area with its unit. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of tries made.
source_tool.art_direction: Cutting squared paper at a desk / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: squared paper with equal square cells, rulers marked in centimetres, unit cubes that stack into rows, layers and cuboids, open boxes, and clear jars of water with a level line.
Every figure is drawn to one scale inside its stage, so a side twice as long looks twice as long, and every square cell and every unit cube in one picture is the same size.
Every side, edge and measure carries its unit: cm or m for a length, sq. cm or sq. m for an area, and cu. cm or cu. m for a volume. The longer side of a rectangle is always the one labelled length.
A cuboid is drawn in three visible faces, and a cube only when all its edges are equal. Cubes hidden behind or under others are shown by a see-through layer when they are counted.
A part square on an estimate is marked by its kind, more than half, half or less than half, in words; no cross ever marks a square that is counted.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a walker tracing a boundary, rows of squares filling a rectangle, layers of cubes stacking into a cuboid, or water rising in a jar.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a square, a cube or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a measure plays in a piece of working: the lengths the question gives, as a side, a length, a breadth, a height, an edge or a base area, are deep blue, and the perimeter, area, volume or missing side the working reaches is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The boundary that a perimeter walks round is vermilion. The unit being counted, one unit square, one unit cube, one row or one layer, is violet. The part squares an area estimate rounds, and the space left over where no whole cube fits, are rose. The side, square, cube, layer or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open and is not used here. A square or cube that is not being counted stays warm white inside its outline, and grid lines and unit words are near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Boundary, Unit square, Unit cube, Layer, More than half, Half and Left over, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at the rows against the outline. Too few, or too many?
voice.onNext: A new target. Try a side and see.
voice.opening: A target, and a shape to find.
voice.onFinish: You worked back to a side and put areas together.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Set a target, try sides, or cut a shape.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has drawn an L-shape along the grid lines, cut it into two rectangles with scissors and counted the squares. The tool is what tries side after side against an area, which paper can show only one try at a time.

answer_key.rule: The area of a square is side x side, so its side is the number that times itself gives the area. From a square's perimeter, find the side first, since 4 x side is the perimeter, then the area. A missing breadth is the number that times the length gives the area; check by multiplying back. An L-shape is cut into two rectangles, and their areas are added; either cut gives the same total. Equal squares put together have an area of the count times one square's area.
answer_key.wrong: The child's try stays drawn, and the stage lays the target's outline over it so the rows that fall short or spill past are lit amber; for a cut, the square counted twice or left out is lit amber. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The area of a square is side x side, so look for a number that times itself gives 256.
Try 15: 15 x 15 = 225, which is too small.
items.question: A square has an area of 256 sq. cm. How long is each side?
items.checkpoint: Try numbers in turn until one times itself gives the area.
items.misconception: Halving the area, as if a side were half of it, which gives a side far too long.

steps: First find the side, because 4 x side is the perimeter.
4 x 21 = 84, so each side is 21 m.
The area of a square of side 21 m is 21 x 21 = 441 sq. m.
items.question: A square yard has a perimeter of 84 m. What is its area?
items.checkpoint: Go through the side: side first, area second.
items.misconception: Multiplying the perimeter by itself, which mixes a length round the edge with a surface.

steps: Area is length x breadth, so 19 x breadth gives 152.
Try 7: 19 x 7 = 133, which is too small.
Try 8: 19 x 8 = 152, so the breadth is 8 cm.
Check it: the area of a 19 cm by 8 cm rectangle is 152 sq. cm.
items.question: A rectangle has an area of 152 sq. cm and a length of 19 cm. How wide is it?
items.misconception: Taking the length away from the area, which mixes a surface with a length.

steps: Cut the floor along the dashed line into two rectangles.
The area of a 14 m by 6 m rectangle is 14 x 6 = 84 sq. m.
The area of an 8 m by 3 m rectangle is 8 x 3 = 24 sq. m.
84 + 24 = 108, so the floor is 108 sq. m.
items.question: An L-shaped floor is cut into a 14 m by 6 m rectangle and an 8 m by 3 m rectangle. What is its area?
items.checkpoint: Cut into rectangles, find each area, then add.
items.misconception: Multiplying the two longest outside sides together, which counts a corner that is not part of the floor.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A square has an area of 16 sq. cm. How long is each side?
A rectangle has an area of 27 sq. m and a length of 9 m. How wide is it?
items.final_answer: 9 x 3 = 27, so the breadth is 3 m

items.question: 5 equal squares each have an area of 9 sq. cm. What area do they cover together?
A square has an area of 225 sq. m. How long is each side?
A square card has a perimeter of 40 cm. What is its area?
items.final_answer: 4 x 10 = 40, so each side is 10 cm. The area of a square of side 10 cm is 10 x 10 = 100 sq. cm

items.question: A rectangle has an area of 98 sq. cm and a length of 14 cm. How wide is it?
items.final_answer: 14 x 7 = 98, so the breadth is 7 cm

items.question: An L-shaped patch is cut into a 16 m by 5 m rectangle and a 9 m by 2 m rectangle. What is its area?
items.final_answer: The first part is 16 x 5 = 80 sq. m. The second part is 9 x 2 = 18 sq. m. 80 + 18 = 98, so the patch is 98 sq. m

items.question: A figure is made of 12 equal squares, each with an area of 9 sq. cm. What is its area?

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

teaching_notes: Cut an L-shape from squared paper into two rectangles before the tool opens, and count its squares to check. To find a side from an area, try small numbers in turn until one times itself gives the area. From a perimeter to an area, always go through the side. A missing breadth is the number that times the length gives the area; multiply back to check. An L-shape may be cut either way, and both cuts give the same total. Equal squares put together have the count times one square's area. The printed squares, rectangles and L-shape are the child's to work.
generation_prompt: Build a work back and split tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A target card gives the measure the question hands over, deep blue, labelled Given. A Try dial draws a square of the chosen side filled with violet rows, labelled Row, against the target's outline, so a try falls short or spills past. A vermilion perimeter string, labelled Boundary, folds into four equal sides with a Fold in four button. A Breadth dial stacks rows on a rectangle of known length until they meet the area, and a Check line multiplies back. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening.
